flawed_step: Step 2 fails: for distinct x,y, T1 gives open neighborhoods X\{y} of x and X\{x} of y, but it does not make them disjoint; their intersection is X\{x,y}, which may be nonempty.
counterexample: Let X=Z with the cofinite topology: U is open iff U is empty or Z\U is finite. Every singleton {n} is closed because its complement Z\{n} is open, so X is T1. However, any two nonempty open sets U and V have finite complements, so Z\(U∩V)=(Z\U)∪(Z\V) is finite. Hence U∩V is cofinite and therefore nonempty. In particular, the distinct points 0 and 1 cannot have disjoint open neighborhoods. Thus X is not Hausdorff.
assessment_summary: The natural proof attempt obtains separate open neighborhoods from the T1 condition but cannot prove they are disjoint. The cofinite topology on Z is an explicit T1, non-Hausdorff counterexample, so the statement is false.
